title: Target Trades at a Fraction of Walmart's Valuation. Is the Discount Deserved?
detail:
Target Trades at a Fraction of Walmart's Valuation. Is the Discount Deserved?
Anders Bylund, The Motley Fool

TGT

NVDA

Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) and Target (NYSE: TGT) sell overlapping goods to overlapping shoppers, but investors price their stocks very differently.

The retail giant from Arkansas has a $992 billion market cap, 13 times Target's. Walmart trades at 45.2 times trailing earnings, Target at 17.1. On price to free cash flow, the gap is wider: 73.3 for Walmart, 16.8 for Target. Both comparisons need a caveat, because both retailers received large tariff refunds last quarter.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The refund asterisk

Target booked a $994 million tariff refund in the Q2 2026 quarter, worth $1.65 of its $4.11 in EPS. Without that one-time benefit, earnings grew about 20% rather than 100%, and the P/E on full-year guidance is nearer 18.8.

Walmart got roughly $2.9 billion in refunds of its own. The company booked the tariff windfall but is plowing much of it back into lower prices, expanding its rollback program from 7,200 to 11,000 items. Management guided Q3 2027's operating income growth to just 2%-4%. At the midpoint of Walmart's EPS guidance, which still includes some refund benefit, the stock trades near 44 times earnings.

Target: real progress, unevenly spread

Target's adjusted 20% bottom-line growth is real, but it's also a bit of a gimme, and the analysis deserves another footnote.

Last year's second quarter was ugly, full of markdowns and costs from canceled vendor orders. Year-over-year comparisons against that modest base were always going to be easy. Still, Target's traffic rose 3.6% in Q2 2026, and traffic from AI platforms like Alphabet's Google Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT is growing at 3.5 times the industry rate (from a tiny base, to be fair). Target's agentic shopping experiment is off to a solid start.

Target is trying to reclaim its classic position as the place for a little extra style on a limited budget. It's not a smooth success, though. Home and apparel, in the words of the chief merchandising officer, are "not where it needs to be."

Walmart: the compounding machine

Walmart, meanwhile, is acting like a tech company that just happens to sell bananas, too. On the most recent earnings call, CFO John David Rainey said almost half of last quarter's profit growth came from membership, advertising, and marketplace.

And the tech effort is fueling real results. Users of the Sparky AI shopping assistant are up 70% and spend 40% more per order, 3,100 U.S. stores receive some automated freight, and automated facilities handle more than half of Walmart's e-commerce fulfillment volume.

title: Walmart earnings growth potential extends beyond headline sales, UBS argues

Walmart earnings growth potential extends beyond headline sales, UBS argues

Walmart earnings growth potential extends beyond headline sales, UBS argues Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

UBS has raised its price target for Walmart Inc (NYSE:WMT, XETRA:WMT) to $149 from $130, arguing its earnings growth potential is stronger than headline sales figures suggest.

The bank expects the US retail giant's third-quarter results to demonstrate continued market share gains, resilient profitability and growing contributions from higher-margin businesses.

UBS believes Walmart can meet or modestly exceed expectations for US comparable sales growth of between 2% and 3%, supported by positive customer traffic and robust eCommerce expansion.

The broker argues that recent price investments should deliver benefits beyond the immediate sales impact by strengthening Walmart's value perception and attracting new customers.

Lower prices can initially increase sales volumes, but the resulting growth must be sufficient to offset the impact of deflation on reported revenue.

UBS nevertheless identified potential pressure on domestic gross margins from changes in retail inventory method accounting and higher freight costs.

The bank estimates additional freight expenses of US$650 million in the quarter and forecasts a 16-basis-point year-on-year change in gross margin as a proportion of net sales.

Consensus expectations assume flat margins, although UBS believes Walmart's underlying US gross margin could still benefit from 30 to 50 basis points of typical expansion.

The broker's broader investment case centres on the growth of eCommerce and alternative revenue streams, which are generating earnings beyond those captured by traditional comparable sales measures.

These businesses could allow Walmart to continue investing in lower prices and convenience while delivering attractive operating income growth.

UBS expects analysts to raise earnings estimates by between US$0.03 and US$0.05 following the results, potentially prompting Walmart to increase its existing financial year earnings per share guidance of US$2.80 to US$2.87.

However, the broker cautioned that the results might not significantly move the shares given their recent performance and elevated valuation.

Walmart trades at approximately 39 times its calendar 2027 earnings per share, reflecting investor enthusiasm for its defensive qualities and consistent growth prospects.

UBS has increased the valuation multiple underpinning its price target to approximately 40 times calendar 2028 earnings, from 35 times previously.

The revised target reflects confidence that Walmart can sustain earnings growth through market share gains, digital expansion and businesses with stronger margins, rather than relying solely on comparable sales growth.

title: Colgate vs. Chipotle: Which Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Should investors stick with a defensive staple or reach for high-growth fast-casual? We compare Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) and Chipotle Mexican Grill (NYSE:CMG) to see which stock might better serve your portfolio by 2027.

Colgate-Palmolive dominates the global personal care market with daily necessities, while Chipotle revolutionizes the restaurant industry with its fresh, fast-casual model. Both companies enjoy strong brand loyalty but operate in vastly different economic climates. This comparison examines their financial health and valuations to help you navigate these distinct investment paths.

The case for Colgate-Palmolive

Colgate-Palmolive operates a global business centered on daily essentials like toothpaste, soap, and pet nutrition. The company reaches consumers in more than 200 countries and employs more than 34,000 people to maintain its massive distribution network. Its primary strategy focuses on delivering consistent growth through leadership in the oral care and pet health categories. Walmart and its affiliates accounted for nearly 11% of net sales in 2025, a concentration that adds risk to the business.

On a trailing-12-month (TTM) basis through the September quarter, revenue reached $21 billion, representing a growth rate of roughly 6% over the prior year. Net income was $2 billion, reflecting steady operational performance. Such results help the company maintain its reputation as a reliable player among consumer staples stocks for conservative investors.

Its September 2026 balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 12x. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, and high values suggest a company uses significant debt to fund its operations. The current ratio is roughly 1.0x, indicating the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets.

TTM free cash flow reached nearly $3.8 billion for the fiscal year, representing cash generated after accounting for spending to maintain or expand physical assets.

The case for Chipotle Mexican Grill

Chipotle Mexican Grill has built its brand around fresh, responsibly sourced ingredients and a fast-casual dining experience. The company operated over 4,200 restaurants by mid-2026 and continues to expand through both digital channels and international licensing. Its growth strategy involves placing an apprentice in every restaurant to strengthen its leadership pipeline by the end of 2027.

TTM revenue reached $12.7 billion, representing approximately 8% growth over the previous year. Net income was close to $1.4 billion, slightly down from the year-ago period's roughly $1.5 billion. These results were driven by a combination of new restaurant openings, increased efficiency at existing locations, and higher labor and other operating costs.
